NEW PATIENT VISIT

51M demolition laborer transferring care; prior PCP in Springfield retired. Records reviewed (abstract in chart).

HPI: Here to establish. Carries a diagnosis of COPD made clinically by his old doctor years ago; as far as he knows he never had breathing tests, and none are in the records. Uses fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 one inhalation twice a day, fairly consistent, and albuterol a few times a week, more with exertion at work. Gets short of breath carrying loads up stairs on jobs, says it has been like that for a while. Morning cough most days, which he attributes to smoking. No recent flares, no ED visits, no oral steroids this year that he recalls. Hypertension on HCTZ 25 for years, no side effects, does not check at home.

Tobacco: 1 ppd since age 13, about 38 pack-years. Never seriously tried to quit.
Alcohol: 1-2 drinks a month. No drugs.
Work: demolition crew for a commercial contractor, a lot of dust; admits he usually skips the mask.
Lives in Chicopee.

PMH: COPD, HTN, tobacco use.
PSH: tonsillectomy age 12.
Meds: as above, reconciled.
Allergies: NKDA.
FHx: father lung cancer dx at 68, deceased. Mother COPD. Brother HTN.
Screening: colonoscopy 2017 normal, due 2027.

ROS: chronic morning cough, exertional dyspnea as above. Denies chest pain, hemoptysis, weight change, fevers, leg swelling.

Exam: BP 132/80, HR 75, SpO2 94% RA, T 36.6, Wt 80.0 kg, Ht 178.6 cm, BMI 25.1.
Well appearing, talkative. Smells of smoke. Neck supple, no LAD. Lungs: clear, no wheeze or crackles. CV: regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs. Abd soft, nontender. Ext: no edema, no cyanosis.

A/P
1. COPD, clinical diagnosis, never confirmed by spirometry. Symptoms stable on ICS/LABA + PRN SABA. Continue fluticasone-salmeterol and albuterol, refills sent. Will look at getting formal PFTs at some point.
2. HTN, at goal on HCTZ 25. BMP today.
3. Tobacco use disorder, 1 ppd. Talked through the link with his lungs and his father's cancer. He listened but is not ready to set a quit date. Offered patch or varenicline whenever he wants them.
4. Health maintenance: Tdap today (last Td 2007). Lipids, BMP, one-time HCV and HIV screening today. Flu shot when available in the fall. PHQ-2 negative.

RTC 6 months, sooner as needed. Gave him the practice cell number for texts.

PULMONARY CONSULTATION
Visit date: 11/16/2020
Referred by: primary care, for COPD evaluation

Reason for referral: COPD carried as a clinical diagnosis without spirometry; recurrent chest infections.

History: Mr. Rossi is a 54-year-old demolition worker. His breathing has been getting worse; he now gets winded climbing one flight of stairs. He coughs every day and brings up yellowish phlegm, most of it first thing in the morning. No fever, chills or chest pain. Over the last year he has needed antibiotics for several chest infections, treated at urgent care. His primary care physician saw him in July for a physical and tobacco counseling.
He continues to smoke a pack a day and tells me he is not ready to stop. Works in construction around a lot of dust and wears a mask only now and then.

Medications: fluticasone propionate/salmeterol 250/50 one inhalation BID; albuterol HFA 2 puffs q4-6h PRN; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily.
Allergies: none known.
Family history: father with lung cancer (age 68), mother with COPD, brother with hypertension.

Examination: BP 131/81, pulse 66, SpO2 96% at rest on room air, weight 80.0 kg. Barrel-shaped chest. Breath sounds decreased throughout with scattered rhonchi. Nicotine staining of the fingernails. No digital clubbing. No cyanosis. Heart sounds regular. No leg edema.

Data:
- Sputum cultures: negative.
- Blood work today: unremarkable.
- Chest radiograph: hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms.
- PFTs: airflow obstruction, only partly reversible after bronchodilator.
- Six-minute walk: limited by breathlessness, and his oxygen saturation fell during the walk.

Impression: COPD, now confirmed by spirometry, with a chronic bronchitis phenotype (daily productive cough) and frequent infectious exacerbations. Ongoing tobacco use and occupational dust exposure.

Recommendations:
1. Smoking cessation discussed at length; he declined a quit date.
2. Continue his current long-term inhaled regimen.
3. Referral placed to pulmonary rehabilitation.
4. Pulmonary follow-up in one year, sooner if needed.

Thank you for involving us in his care.
Pulmonology

documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
PULMONARY FOLLOW-UP
Visit date: 11/26/2021

Mr. Rossi returns one year after his initial evaluation for COPD. He has no complaints today and his breathing is at its baseline. What brought him in was worry about lung cancer: he still smokes and his father died of it.

Current medications: fluticasone propionate/salmeterol 250/50 BID, albuterol PRN, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily.
Social: current smoker, one pack daily since age 13, approximately 42 pack-years.

Exam: BP 134/82, HR 77, SpO2 95% RA, weight 79.7 kg. His examination is unremarkable today.

Assessment:
1. COPD, stable.
2. High risk for lung cancer: age 55, about 42 pack-years, currently smoking. He meets criteria for annual low-dose CT screening.

Discussion: We talked through what screening with low-dose CT involves. I explained that many scans find small nodules that turn out to be benign, so a positive scan often leads to repeat imaging and occasionally a procedure, and that a negative scan does not remove all risk. We also discussed that the size at which a nodule is called positive is a choice: a lower size cut-off catches more cancers but labels more people with benign nodules as positive, and a higher one does the opposite. He asked good questions about what a positive result would mean for him, and after this conversation he would like to proceed. We also talked again about quitting, which would do more for his risk than any scan.

Plan:
- Low-dose CT lung cancer screening, annually. I would be grateful if your office would place the order so the results come to you.
- Continue current inhalers.
- Follow up in one year or sooner.

Pulmonology

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PROVIDER NOTE
Arrival 11/13/2022 13:05. Disposition 19:40, discharged.

CHIEF COMPLAINT: belly pain, constipation, irritable

HPI: 56-year-old man with COPD and current tobacco use with about six weeks of crampy abdominal pain that has been getting worse, along with constipation and feeling short-tempered. For roughly the past month people he works with have told him he has been irritable and is having a hard time staying on task with his work. He has not traveled and has not changed what he eats. No vomiting, no blood in the stool, no fever.

PMH: COPD, hypertension. Meds: fluticasone/salmeterol 250/50 BID, albuterol PRN, HCTZ 25 mg daily. NKDA.
Social: current smoker. Construction demolition worker.

EXAM: vitals as charted, afebrile.
General: no acute distress.
Abdomen: mild tenderness in the epigastrium, no rebound or guarding, bowel sounds present, no masses.
Neuro: speech is slowed and he is intermittently confused during the interview, but he is oriented to person, place and time. Moves all extremities.
Lungs: clear, no respiratory distress. Heart regular.

RESULTS:
Hgb 9.8, MCV 74. Iron 85, TIBC 360, transferrin saturation 24%, ferritin 110.
Hepatic enzymes and renal function within normal limits.
Peripheral smear (reviewed with lab): microcytic red cells with coarse basophilic stippling.
Abdominal radiograph, 2 views: nonobstructive bowel gas pattern; no free air.

MDM: Microcytic anemia with iron indices that do not suggest iron deficiency, coarse basophilic stippling on smear, abdominal colic, constipation and neurocognitive change in a demolition worker raise concern for lead toxicity. No obstruction on imaging; abdominal exam benign. Venous blood lead level sent; it is a send-out and will not result today. He is safe for discharge with close primary care follow-up; his PCP practice was messaged.

DISPOSITION: Discharged home. Follow up with PCP in 1-2 days for lead level result. Return for worsening pain, vomiting, confusion, weakness or seizure.

Do not return to work tasks that involve cutting, torching or sanding painted surfaces until you are cleared. ED 11/13: abdominal pain, constipation, irritability. Hgb 9.8, MCV 74, iron 85/TIBC 360/sat 24%/ferritin 110 (not iron deficient), smear with coarse basophilic stippling, KUB without obstruction. Venous blood lead 62 µg/dL resulted 11/15.

Today: cramping and constipation still there but milder. Coworkers had been on him about being short-tempered and losing track of tasks; he notices it less this week. No headache, no weakness in hands or feet, no vomiting.
Exposure: for about two months he has been torch-cutting and grinding painted structural steel on a mill demolition. Respirator only sometimes. Eats lunch on site. No hobbies with lead (no shooting, casting, stained glass). Lives alone, no kids at home.

BP 129/79, HR 66, SpO2 94%, wt 79.9 kg.
Alert and oriented, conversant, speech normal rate today, follows multistep commands. No gum line discoloration. Abdomen soft, mild epigastric tenderness, no rebound. Strength 5/5 grips and wrist extensors bilaterally. Lungs clear, no crackles.

A/P
1. Lead poisoning, occupational, BLL 62 µg/dL with anemia and GI/neurocognitive symptoms. Remove from exposure is the main treatment. Not pursuing chelation at this level with improving symptoms; will follow levels. Work note: no lead-exposed tasks until cleared. Reported to the state occupational lead surveillance program as required. Repeat blood lead and CBC in 4 weeks. Hygiene counseling: wash hands/face before eating or smoking, change clothes and boots before getting in the truck, wash work clothes separately.
2. Microcytic anemia - due to lead; recheck with BLL.
3. Tobacco use disorder - smoking with lead-dusted hands adds to the exposure; he says he will at least stop smoking on site. Still declines a quit date.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Pt texted asking whether his shoulder could be "a pinched nerve." Called him.
Three months of right shoulder pain, deep and constant, no injury he can think of. Over the past few weeks tingling into the right hand, and the hand feels weaker - dropping tools. He also mentions his cough has been bringing up streaks of blood on and off.
In a 57-year-old with ~44 pack-years, an apical lung process has to be excluded before anything musculoskeletal. His last screening CT was 12/2022 (negative); next is not due until December.
Called pulmonology: they moved his routine follow-up up to Monday 11/13 and will get a chest film that day and image further from there. Pt agrees. Told him to go to the ED for heavy bleeding, shortness of breath or new weakness.

documents.title: Pulmonology visit
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
PULMONARY CLINIC NOTE
Date of visit: 11/13/2023 (moved up at the request of his PCP)

Mr. Rossi, 57, with COPD, followed in our lung cancer screening program (last low-dose CT 12/2022, Lung-RADS 1). He describes three months of pain in the right shoulder and, more recently, tingling and weakness in the right hand. There was no trauma. He also has a lingering cough with occasional blood streaking.

Social: current smoker, 40 pack-years. Demolition laborer.
Meds: fluticasone/salmeterol 250/50 BID; albuterol PRN; HCTZ 25 mg daily. NKDA.

Exam: BP 133/81, HR 69, SpO2 96%, weight 79.4 kg.
Right upper eyelid droops and the right pupil is smaller than the left. Sweating over the right side of the face is reduced. Right hand grip is weaker than the left.

Labs today: Hgb 14.2, WBC 7,800, platelets 250,000, sodium 140, potassium 4.2, creatinine 1.0, calcium 9.8.

Chest radiograph today: mass at the apex of the right lung.

Assessment: Right apical lung mass with an ipsilateral Horner pattern (ptosis, miosis, facial anhidrosis) and right hand symptoms - highly concerning for a superior sulcus lung cancer. This appeared within a year of a negative screening CT.

Plan: CT chest with contrast this week. Depending on the result, PET-CT, brain MRI and tissue sampling, which our office will arrange. I discussed the concern for cancer with him directly. We will keep his primary care physician updated.

Pulmonology

reports.text: CT CHEST WITH IV CONTRAST. Indication: right apical mass on radiograph, Horner syndrome. Comparison: low-dose CT 12/19/2022, chest radiograph 11/13/2023. There is a 4.8 cm mass in the apical right upper lobe at the superior sulcus. A right paratracheal lymph node measures 1.6 cm in short axis. Background emphysema. No other pulmonary mass or nodule. No pleural or pericardial effusion. Heart normal in size. Visualized liver and adrenal glands unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: 1. 4.8 cm right upper lobe apical (superior sulcus) mass, highly suspicious for primary lung carcinoma. 2. Enlarged right paratracheal lymph node, 1.6 cm short axis. 3. Emphysema.

documents.title: PET-CT skull base to mid-thigh
documents.author: radiology
documents.body:
FDG PET-CT, SKULL BASE TO MID-THIGH
Date: 11/28/2023
Indication: right upper lobe superior sulcus mass, staging.
Comparison: CT chest 11/17/2023.

Findings: The 4.8 cm right upper lobe apical mass is intensely FDG-avid. The 1.6 cm right paratracheal lymph node is FDG-avid. No other hypermetabolic thoracic lymph nodes. No FDG-avid lesion in the liver, adrenal glands or skeleton. Emphysema. No abnormal uptake in the abdomen or pelvis.

Impression: FDG-avid right upper lobe superior sulcus mass and right paratracheal node. No evidence of distant metastatic disease.

reports.text: MRI BRAIN. Indication: lung cancer staging. Comparison: none. No intracranial mass, hemorrhage or acute infarct. No edema or mass effect. Ventricles and sulci normal for age. Midline structures normal. Orbits and paranasal sinuses unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: Normal MRI of the brain. No evidence of intracranial metastatic disease.

reports.text: SPECIMEN: Lymph node, right paratracheal (station 4R), endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration, with cell block. Adequacy: rapid on-site evaluation adequate, lymphoid tissue present. Microscopic: aspirate smears and cell block contain clusters of malignant epithelial cells with enlarged pleomorphic nuclei, set in a lymphoid background.
reports.conclusion: Lymph node, station 4R, EBUS-TBNA: POSITIVE for malignant cells, non-small cell carcinoma.

documents.title: Bronchoscopy with EBUS-TBNA
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
PROCEDURE: Flexible bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA)
Date: 12/01/2023
Indication: 4.8 cm right upper lobe superior sulcus mass with FDG-avid 1.6 cm right paratracheal node; staging and diagnosis.
Sedation: moderate sedation, monitored.
Findings: Airway inspection normal to the subsegmental level, no endobronchial lesion. EBUS: enlarged right paratracheal (4R) node sampled with 22-gauge needle, multiple passes; rapid on-site evaluation showed malignant cells. Other mediastinal stations not enlarged on ultrasound.
Complications: none. Discharged home same day with escort.

Pathology (final 12/04): station 4R positive for non-small cell carcinoma.

Summary: Non-small cell lung carcinoma of the right upper lobe (superior sulcus) with right paratracheal nodal involvement and no distant disease on PET-CT and brain MRI: clinical stage IIIB, not a surgical candidate. Referred to medical and radiation oncology; consult with medical oncology 12/06. Results discussed with Mr. Rossi today. Copy to PCP.

Pulmonology

documents.title: Medical oncology consultation
documents.author: oncology
documents.body:
MEDICAL ONCOLOGY - NEW PATIENT CONSULTATION
Date: 12/06/2023
Referring: pulmonology. Copy: primary care.

Diagnosis: Non-small cell lung carcinoma, right upper lobe superior sulcus, clinical stage IIIB. 4.8 cm apical mass with FDG-avid 1.6 cm right paratracheal node (EBUS-TBNA 12/01/2023 positive for NSCLC). PET-CT 11/28: no distant metastases. MRI brain 11/29: negative.

History: 57-year-old man with COPD, hypertension and ongoing smoking (pack a day, about 44 pack-years). Three months of right shoulder pain with right hand tingling and weakness; blood-streaked sputum. Demolition laborer; occupational lead poisoning 2022, resolved.
Meds: fluticasone/salmeterol, albuterol, HCTZ. NKDA.
Family history: father with lung cancer.

Exam: BP 129/83, HR 81, SpO2 95%, weight 80.8 kg. Ambulatory, fully independent. Right ptosis and miosis. Right grip mildly weak. Lungs clear bilaterally. No supraclavicular adenopathy. Heart regular. Abdomen benign. No edema.

Assessment and plan:
Unresectable stage IIIB superior sulcus NSCLC. Recommend definitive concurrent chemoradiation: weekly carboplatin (AUC 2) and paclitaxel (45 mg/m2) with thoracic radiation to 60 Gy in 30 fractions, followed by consolidation durvalumab for up to a year if there is no progression. Radiation oncology consult arranged. Chemotherapy teaching scheduled. Target start early January.
I told him plainly that continuing to smoke will work against his treatment, and urged him to stop now; he will think about it.

Medical Oncology

Stage IIIB NSCLC of the right upper lobe, after chemoradiation and seven months of consolidation durvalumab (eighth dose 09/11/2024).

Social: former smoker, quit 04/2024. Alcohol 1-2 drinks a month. Works as a demolition laborer.

Exam: Over the right lower chest, breath sounds are diminished and the percussion note is dull. Clubbing. Right ptosis and miosis.

Pathology: CT-guided biopsy of the mass was done today; final read non-small cell lung carcinoma.
Labs: CBC, CMP, TSH within normal limits.

Assessment: New right lower lobe site of non-small cell lung carcinoma during consolidation durvalumab, in keeping with progression of his known stage IIIB cancer.
Plan:

2. PET-CT 10/03 to restage before deciding on next treatment.
3. Return after PET.

PULMONARY CLINIC
Date: 11/13/2025 (moved up at his request)

Background: stage IIIB NSCLC (right upper lobe superior sulcus) treated with chemoradiation and durvalumab, with SBRT for a right lower lobe site in 10/2024; COPD.

History: For four months he has been losing weight steadily, coughing more and feeling fatigued. Over the past month he has had occasional hemoptysis. He has a 40-pack-year history and quit smoking about a year and a half ago.

Vitals: temperature 37.2 C (99 F), BP 130/80, pulse 88, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 94% on room air, weight 67.1 kg.
Exam: Cachectic. Breath sounds decreased at both apices. Clubbing. Right ptosis and miosis.

Labs: complete blood count and basic metabolic panel normal.
Chest x-ray: cavitary lesions in both upper lobes.
High-resolution CT the same day (done in place of his October surveillance scan): several cavities in both apices; one contains an intracavitary mass suggestive of an aspergilloma.

Assessment: Bilateral apical cavitary disease with a probable aspergilloma, in a man with emphysema and prior thoracic radiation; recurrent malignancy is less likely on this pattern but remains in the differential.
Plan: Aspergillus IgG serology sent today. I will contact him with the result. Copy to oncology and primary care.

ADDENDUM to 11/13/2025 visit
Aspergillus fumigatus IgG returned at 148 mg/L (reference below 40). Together with the bilateral apical cavities and the intracavitary mass on high-resolution CT, this supports pulmonary aspergillosis with aspergilloma. Discussed with the patient by phone today.
Plan:

2. Itraconazole trough level and hepatic panel 2 weeks after starting (target trough at least 1 mg/L); hepatic panel every 3 months after that.

4. Pulmonology clinic follow-up; oncology surveillance imaging continues.
